lines.text: Marinara means sailor-style. Nobody knows for sure why.
Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas in the fifteen-hundreds. Some Italians fried them; plenty of others grew them for looks. They're cousins of deadly nightshade.
In sixteen ninety-two, a Naples steward, Antonio Latini, printed one of the earliest known tomato sauce recipes: Spanish-style, for boiled meat, not pasta.
The sailor stories? They come from tradition, not records.
In Naples, marinara often means a pizza: tomato, garlic, oregano, oil. No cheese. In America, it mostly means the sauce.
Recipe one: microwave marinara. Better than any jar.
A fifteen-ounce can of tomato sauce. I like Cento. Two tablespoons of cheap red wine. Two or three teaspoons of Italian seasoning, rubbed between your palms. A glug of olive oil.
Cover it loosely. Three to four minutes on high, stirring halfway.
Then onion powder, and half as much garlic. No salt; the can's seasoned. Stir. Done.
Recipe two is even better, and there's still nothing to chop.
Oil in a skillet. Tube tomato paste; let it brown. Seasoning, thirty seconds. A splash of wine, maybe balsamic, and cook it down. Then the sauce, onion and garlic.
Now the best part. See the oil pooling at the edge? Sweep your spoon around it, swirl it into the middle, until tiny droplets catch the light.
Save this for pasta night. More recipes coming.
